payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the background into a basketball court
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image show the background changed into a basketball court?
node.criteria: Pass if the background itself is recognizably a basketball court, supported by visible court context such as a playing surface and court markings; basketball equipment may support this judgment but equipment alone is insufficient. Fail if the background is clearly not a basketball court. Unknown if the background cannot be assessed reliably.
node.binding: Judge whether the requested background replacement is complete: the background must read as a basketball court, not merely contain basketball-related objects.

node_traces.evidence: The background has been changed from a kitchen and includes basketball hoops and balls, but it does not read as a basketball court: there is no recognizable court surface or visible court markings beyond a single line.

The kitchen background has been replaced with a dark basketball-themed scene, but it does not read as a basketball court: there is no recognizable playing surface with court markings. The hoops and basketballs alone are insufficient.

The kitchen background has been replaced with basketball-related objects, including a hoop and basketballs, but the background does not read as a basketball court: there is no recognizable court playing surface or clear court markings.
The background shows a basketball hoop and a playing surface with visible court markings, so it reads as a basketball court.

The edited background shows a basketball hoop and balls, but the surrounding area is a plain dark backdrop with no recognizable basketball-court playing surface or markings. Basketball equipment alone does not establish a court.

fulfillment: The binding is underspecified: “Target: The background (...) a basketball court” does not clearly distinguish a complete court background from basketball-themed objects or partial court cues. Make the completion criterion explicitly assess whether the background as a whole reads as a court, using the visible playing surface and court markings as evidence; treat hoops or balls alone as progress, not completion. Preserve the existing partial-progress logic: s1 determines completion and s2 can establish requested progress when s1 fails. The edited image shows a hoop, balls, and a court-like floor/line, but much of the background is plain dark, so the disagreement is about whether those cues make the setting recognizable—not absence of all progress. The traces repeatedly assign high-confidence partial despite differing descriptions of the floor and markings, and one trace conflicts internally about s2; clarify how dependencies map to completion versus progress and require evidence-based resolution of such conflicts rather than treating confidence or repetition as proof. No transport or schema failure is reported.
s2: Refine this support node so it tests requested progress, not whether the edit is complete: completion belongs to parent s1, and s2 should pass when visible background changes are recognizably directed toward a basketball court but remain incomplete. Bind the judgment to the background as a scene, distinguishing court-setting evidence (playing surface and court markings) from basketball props alone; do not require the whole frame to read as a finished court to count partial progress. In this image, the kitchen has been replaced by a dark backdrop with a hoop and balls, plus a bright court-like floor and line, so assess those cues together rather than claiming either no progress or a complete court. Clarify that s2’s fail means no discernible requested progress, not “the change is complete”; route completion to s1 and ensure the parent interprets s1/s2 outcomes consistently. When evidence about the floor or markings is uncertain or conflicting, use unknown or lower confidence and state the visual basis—repeated high-confidence judgments are not independent evidence. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated.
